kernels.definition: A function is a named, reusable block of code defined with def that runs only when it is called; variables created inside it are local to that call.

definitionAnchor.quote: A function is a named, reusable block of code that performs a task when called

facts.text: A function is defined with the def keyword, a name, parentheses, and a colon, with an indented body.

anchor.quote: A function is defined using the def keyword

facts.text: A variable's scope is the part of the program where it can be accessed.

anchor.quote: A variable's scope is the part of a program where the variable can be accessed

facts.text: A variable created inside a function has local scope and cannot be accessed outside the function.

anchor.quote: A variable created within a function has local scope and only exists within the function

facts.text: A variable created outside any function has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program.

anchor.quote: A variable created outside of a function has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §6.1 Defining functions; §6.3 Variable scope

kernels.definition: A list is an ordered collection of values written in square brackets; each element has an index, beginning at 0.

definitionAnchor.quote: A list object can be used to bundle elements together in Python

facts.text: A list is written with square brackets [] holding comma-separated values.

anchor.quote: A list is defined by using square brackets [] with comma separated values within the square brackets

facts.text: Individual elements are accessed directly using an index.

anchor.quote: Individual list elements can be accessed directly using an index

facts.text: Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence.

anchor.quote: Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence

facts.text: A for loop can iterate through a list, visiting each element in order.

anchor.quote: An iterative for loop can be used to iterate through a list

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §3.4 List basics; §9.1 Modifying and iterating lists

kernels.definition: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position.

definitionAnchor.quote: A dictionary in Python is a container object including key-value pairs

facts.text: Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.

anchor.quote: a dictionary object cannot hold duplicate key values

facts.text: Dictionaries are written with curly braces in key: value form and are ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered.

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §10.1 Dictionary basics

mcItems.q: Which statement accurately describes the scope of a variable defined within a function?
op: It has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program.
It has local scope and cannot be accessed outside the function.
It is accessible globally if defined with the def keyword.
It has the same scope as variables defined outside any function.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is that a variable created inside a function has local scope and cannot be accessed outside the function. The misconception is believing that variables defined inside a function retain global scope, which is incorrect.

mcItems.q: Where can a variable created outside any function be accessed?
op: Only within the function where it was defined.
Anywhere in the program.
Only in the immediate block following its creation.
Only in the function where it is first used.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is that a variable created outside any function has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program. The misconception is assuming that variables defined outside a function are restricted to the function where they were initially created.

mcItems.q: Which data structure is best suited for representing data where items are naturally labeled rather than ordered?
op: List, because it maintains a numeric position.
Dictionary, because it uses key-value pairs.
Tuple, because it enforces a fixed order.
Array, because it stores sequential data.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is Dictionary because it is ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered. A common misconception is choosing a List because it maintains a numeric position, which is incorrect as lists are ordered by index.

mcItems.q: If a data structure cannot hold duplicate keys, which structure is it?
op: List, because it allows multiple identical elements.
Array, because it stores elements sequentially.
Dictionary, because it looks up values by unique keys.
Set, because it only stores unique values.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is Dictionary because because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys. A common misconception is choosing a List because it allows multiple identical elements, which is incorrect as lists can contain duplicate values.

keyTerms.df: The process of associating a unique identifier with a piece of data.
keyTerms.eg: Storing student scores where the student ID is the key and the score is the value.
keyTerms.mi: Thinking that the data must be stored in a strictly sequential, ordered manner.
keyTerms.cx: Data is stored based on a label (key) rather than a numerical position.

keyTerms.df: The constraint that every identifier used to access a stored item must be distinct.
keyTerms.eg: Ensuring that in a dictionary, no two entries share the same label.
keyTerms.mi: Assuming that the structure can accommodate multiple entries with the same label.
keyTerms.cx: Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.
